The letters that open this surah, the disjointed letters (huruf muqatta'at), are, in our view in their interpretation, the same letters from which the Qur'an is composed. It is from these very letters that this inimitable Book has been formed, and humanity is unable to bring a book like it. After the mention of these letters, the story of Prophet Zakariyya (Zechariah) and Yahya (John) begins. Most of the material of this story is based on the mercy of Allah. The whole atmosphere is overshadowed by the mercy of God. Thus the beginning itself is with the word "mercy," the mention of mercy...
The original story begins with the scene of a prayer. This prayer is made by Hazrat Zakariyya (Zechariah), and he makes it with great humility and with reverence and lowliness of heart.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 3:

They engage in private supplication to their Lord, away from the eyes of people. No one sees them, no one hears them. In the corner of solitude, with utmost sincerity, they call upon their Lord and open their hearts before their Lord (who knows well), placing before Allah their burden and their anxiety. They call upon their Lord in a state of the closest intimacy and union (Rabb). Here they do not even bring in the particle of address (ya). Allah hears and sees even without supplication; He has no need of the calling of anyone who calls. Rather, it is a need of a grieving person that he call out, that he complain, and Allah is Merciful and Generous. He created human beings, and He knows that calling out, weeping and complaining also lightens the burden of this creature. Therefore Allah has commanded: make supplication, entreat, and bring out from yourselves whatever weighs upon your hearts.

"And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you" (Qur'an 40:60). This is so that some weight may be lifted from your nerves, and so that your hearts may be assured that we have reported to a Being who is stronger, a Being of great power, the Absolute Omnipotent. And so that you may become aware that your connection is with the One before whom no request is disappointed, and whoever places his trust in Him never fails.

Prophet Zakariyya complains before his Lord that his bones have become weak, and when the bones become weak the whole body becomes weak, for the bones are indeed the strongest part of the body; the basic framework of the body stands upon the bones. Then he complains of the whiteness of his hair. Observe the manner of expression: it is as though whiteness is a fire that has caught the hair of the head; the head is burning rapidly in it, and soon no black hair will remain.

The loosening of the bones and the whitening of the head's hair are both metaphors for old age and the weakness and frailty he is afflicted with, and yet he is not hopeless of Allah's mercy. He presents his petition.

And alongside this, before the acceptance of supplication, they also make their own commentary.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 7:

The scene of the acceptance of this prayer is painted in an atmosphere of great tenderness, affection and divine pleasure. From the higher realm, the Lord of Majesty Himself calls out to His servant: "Yā Zakariyyā" (O Zakariyya), and at the very moment of calling, the glad tidings are given: ﴿Indeed, We give you good news of a boy﴾ (19:7). Then Allah reaches the very limit of grace: the name of the boy is also designated from the higher realm: ﴿whose name is Yahya﴾ (19:7), and moreover, no one before him had been given this name: ﴿We have not made for him before, any namesake﴾ (19:7).

This is the outpouring and rain of Allah's bounty, which He showers upon His servant who called upon Him with utmost humility. He called in secret, and laid open his heart before his Lord, saying that his bones had weakened. He placed his problem before Allah. What had compelled him to make this supplication was that he feared his relatives and companions, that they would not be able to properly uphold the trust of the Islamic way of life and the financial management. Allah bestowed His favour upon him, fulfilled his wish, and made him content.

Since his prayer was accepted immediately, the fervour of his desire for offspring instantly cooled, and the warmth of hope turned into certainty. Suddenly he found himself confronted with a real situation: how this matter would actually be accomplished. He is an old man, dried up, his bones have become loose, and his head is white. Moreover, his wife is barren, and in her youth she bore him no children; now how can she bear a child? Therefore, a desire for further assurance is natural. So he asks to know how and through what means this child will come about.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 8:

Qala rabbi anna yakunu li ghulamun wa kanati imra'ati 'aqiran wa qad balaghtu minal-kibri 'ita'iyya (19:8). ﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ "He said: 'O my Lord! How shall I have a son, when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age and become dried up?'" Since he was faced with a practical situation, and since there is Allah's promise, and it is true, he is fully certain that this will happen. Yet he wishes to know the manner in which this promise will become a reality under present circumstances, so that his heart may be at peace. This is a natural and innate psychological state. Prophet Zakariyya (peace be upon him) was a righteous prophet, but he was also a human being and a realistic person. He wants to know how exactly Allah will change the actual circumstances.

Allah's response answers this as well: O servant, this matter is not difficult. Just look at your own self, how you came into existence when you were not there at all. Every individual's case is the same. Every living thing in this universe was not, and then came to be.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 9:

He said: "So it will be." Your Lord says: "That is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing." (19:9)

In the creation of His creatures, nothing is difficult for Allah. The small and the great, the insignificant and the magnificent, all have their cause in the single word "Kun" (Be). When Allah decrees something, it comes to be.

It is Allah who has made the barren woman such that she has no offspring, and who has made the aged such that the continuation of progeny ceases through them. He can also set right the barren woman, remove her barrenness, and bring back procreative power into an aged man. And this task is easier, in comparison to the fact that Allah created man when he was nothing, for Allah it is no difficulty to bring into being something from the beginning or to repeat it.

Despite all these realities, Prophet Zakariyya is so eager for complete reassurance that he asks for a sign for this unexpected event, so that when this glad tiding becomes manifest in fact, he will know what its sign will be. So Allah set for this glad tidings a sign that is in harmony with the atmosphere in which the Prophet had first made this supplication and had been answered, so that Zakariyya might, through this sign, also give thanks to the Lord, the Exalted, that Allah gave him a child in this old age. He would be cut off from the world of people and devote three days solely to Allah. During those days his tongue would be able to speak only in the glorification of Allah, and if he wished to speak to people, his tongue would be restrained, though his limbs would be sound. Nor would his tongue be afflicted with any problem.

He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, though you are sound." So it happened.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 11:

﴿So he came out to his people from the sanctuary, and he signaled to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening.﴾ (19:11)

So he went out to his people from the sanctuary (mihrab) and, by a sign, instructed them: glorify (Allah) morning and evening. This was so that they too might enter into that atmosphere and that state into which he had entered, and that they too might give thanks to Allah together with him, because Allah had shown favour to him and to them, since this boy would, after them, become their imam (leader) and guide.

Here the Qur'an leaves Zakariyya in his state of silence; the curtain falls, the page of that scene is folded up, and when the next scene comes into view, Yahya himself is coming forward, and the call of his Lord comes to him from the higher realm.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 12:

﴿Yahya, take hold of the Book with determination.﴾ (19:12) Yahya was born, passed through childhood, and reached youth, and all of this took place in the gap between these two scenes. This is the particular artistic style of the Qur'an: it presents the important links of an event, in which life and activity are vivid, while the unimportant links are left to the human mind.

Yahya is called with the word of address (kalimah al-nida'), and only afterwards is he spoken to, because the scene of calling someone out loud is a very appealing image, and it shows the station Yahya holds in the higher realm. Moreover, the answering of Zakariya's supplication was a very significant event. His supplication was that he should have an heir who would be his successor and manage the office of leadership well, both in terms of the ideology and in terms of the family responsibilities. Accordingly, this charge is being given to Yahya so that he may fulfil his responsibilities as Zakariya had asked.

﴿Yahya, take hold of the Book with determination.﴾ (19:12) By "the Book" is meant the Torah, which was the book of the Children of Israel after Musa (peace be upon him). The prophets of the Children of Israel would carry this book, act upon it, and judge according to it. Yahya was the heir of his father Zakariya, so he was called upon to take up this burden and to rise with strength and resolve, to take hold of this trust, not to be lax in this task, not to show any weakness, and not to shrink back from the responsibilities of this inheritance.

After this call, it is told how Allah had bestowed upon Yahya such a personality so that he could discharge the responsibilities of the office of leadership.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah Maryam (19), verses 13–15:

"And We gave him wisdom while still a child, and tenderness from Us and purity, and he was deeply pious." This was the capability with which Allah had blessed him, and in this way he was helped to carry out the responsibilities of the office of successor (khilafah) to Zakariyya.

He was given wisdom (hikmah) while still a child, so he was also unrivalled in ability, just as he was distinguished in his name and in his birth. Wisdom, which in anyone comes after great experience, was granted to Yahya (ʿalayhi al-salam) in his childhood.

Furthermore, tenderness of heart was granted to him from birth, so he had no need to exert himself to express it, nor any need to train himself and make this conduct a second nature through practice. Rather, at the time of his birth it was his second nature. Tenderness of heart is a basic quality for every responsible person, and especially for a prophet, so that he may gather various people around him, that deep love for him may arise in people's hearts, and that they may come to him willingly.

Allah granted him purity, chastity and inner cleanliness. Through these he would cleanse the rancour of hearts and the impurities of hearts, and he would carry out the work of purification and moral cleansing among the common people.

"Wa kana taqiyyan" (31): "And he was deeply pious." He was devoted to Allah (mawsul billah), fearful of Allah, one who kept Allah constantly before his eyes, one who feared Him and who was mindful of Allah's watchfulness. He knew that Allah sees the outward and the inward. This was the provision for the journey that Allah had given to Yahya in childhood, so that he would be the successor (khalifah) of his father, for which Zakariyya had turned to Allah and prayed earnestly, and the Lord had accepted that prayer and bestowed upon him this pure child.

Here Yahya too disappears suddenly from the scene, and the curtain falls, just as earlier Zakariyya (ʿalayhi al-salam) had suddenly gone into the background. But in a few glimpses, the outlines of his life have been drawn, and his inclinations and manner of life have been shown. The purpose of the whole story was two scenes: Zakariyya's prayer and the divine announcement of its acceptance. This purpose has been fulfilled in a few words, through calling Yahya from the higher realm and mentioning his ability and capacity. Therefore there was no need to give details or to record every single event. If anyone now were to narrate many events of Yahya's life, it would add nothing to the purpose of the story.

Now the Qur'an turns to a birth even stranger than the birth of Yahya. This is the story of the birth of ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam). The flow of the discourse, having presented the striking scene of a child born to a barren woman and an aged, decrepit man, now gradually leads the readers to a far more wondrous event, one about which there has been much disagreement. In this second event, the more astonishing thing is that a child was born without a father to a virgin.

Setting aside the creation of humanity itself and of Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam), the birth of ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam) is a great wonder in the history of humankind. It is an event for which there is no parallel, neither before ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam) in history nor after him.

A greater wonder than the birth of ʿIsa is the creation of Adam himself, but at that time humanity did not yet exist, so that Allah created the first human without father or mother. Human beings came later and did not witness the creation of Adam. The divine will desired that this second wonder should take place before the eyes of people: that ʿIsa should be born without a father, and that, departing from the pattern according to which human beings have been settled on this earth and according to which the chain of human procreation continues, an event should occur which people could see with their own eyes, and which would be so well known, distinguished and unforgettable that coming generations for centuries would take a lesson from it, because the first miracle and wonder occurred before the existence of humankind.

Allah established a sunnah for all His creatures: that all kinds of living beings continue according to a fixed sunnah of reproduction, and that this chain proceeds through male and female. Even in things where there is no male and female, the reproductive cells of both sexes have been placed in a single individual. This sunnah has been running for centuries and has settled thoroughly in the human mind. Humanity has come to think that perhaps this is the only possible way of creation. It has forgotten the creation of Adam, how the first human came into being. If this matter lies somewhat beyond human thought and observation, Allah, by creating ʿIsa without a father, showed that Allah is not Himself bound by the sunnah He has established. Allah's will is free, His power is unrestricted, and His will is not bound to any form or method. Yet an event like that of ʿIsa did not continue, because the sunnah Allah had established for this universe was to continue. The event of ʿIsa was not meant to change the enduring sunnah of reproduction for humanity. For the proof of Allah's power, His will and the freedom of His decree, this single example was sufficient to show that Allah is not Himself bound by the laws He has established.

"Wa linaj'alahu ayatan lil-nas" (And that We may make him a sign for people).

Because this event was strange and extraordinary, departing from the sunnah of Allah, some sects could not understand it properly, nor could they grasp the wisdom behind Allah's showing this event. They began attributing divine attributes to ʿIsa ibn Maryam and started weaving a fabric of illusions and superstitions about his birth. They did not try to understand the true purpose Allah had in that creation. Instead of being guided, they went astray. That is, instead of saying that this event shows that divine power is unrestricted, they made ʿIsa himself a god, and their beliefs became corrupted.

In this surah the Qur'an narrates this event in somewhat more detail, states its true purpose, and refutes the superstitions and fables. Its manner of expression is in the form of deeply impactful scenes, full of emotional imagery and human impressions. Whoever reads these scenes carefully and visualises them with the eye of imagination, his hair stands on end and he trembles. Read carefully.

This is the first scene. There is a virgin young woman, extremely chaste and pure. Her mother had dedicated her to the service of the place of worship while she was still in her mother's womb. This woman withdraws from her household and from her family of such purity; her circumstances are such that she is becoming hidden from sight. The context does not explicitly state this fact, because it relates to the particular private matters of virgins.

She is in her seclusion, content with her life, but then she sees that a young man is standing in her room, a complete young man.

Whenever the honour and chastity of a woman is in danger, courage arises naturally within her. Accordingly, Maryam (ʿalayhā al-salām) asks with boldness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 20:

﴿She said: "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ Maryam said: "How can I have a son, when no human being has touched me, and I am not a woman of ill conduct?"

Here she speaks plainly and in clear words, and she and this person are alone together. Suddenly the purpose and aim of this person's appearance has also become apparent. She wants to know how he intends to give her a child. Yes, when he said, "I am the messenger of your Lord," her fear of Him did not prevent her from asking how a child, who would be pure and whose birth would not be through unlawful means, and whose character would not be bad, could come to her. Therefore she speaks openly at this very moment, and it is also fitting to ask how this child can be born when no person has touched me, and I am not a woman who sells her chastity, so that people would accept my child as the child of an immoral woman.

From the question and answer up to this point, it becomes clear that Maryam did not believe in any means of birth other than the union of a man and a woman, and this is the natural thought for an ordinary person.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 19, verse 21:

قال کذلک قال ربک ھو علی ھین ولنجعلہ ایۃ للناس و رحمۃ منا (91 : 12) "The angel said, 'So it will be. Your Lord says, "That is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign for mankind and a mercy from Us."'"

This extraordinary manner of birth, which Maryam herself could not have imagined, is easy for Allah. When Allah wishes to bring a thing into existence, He says only "Kun" (Be), and it is. Everything is easy for Allah, whether it comes about through natural means in accordance with the established Divine way (sunnah Ilahiyyah) or through extraordinary means. The angel now makes it clear that this is the command of God: it will be so, and it is easy for me. Allah the Exalted wishes to make this wonder a sign for the people, and to demonstrate that Allah's power, Allah's will, and His purpose are unrestrained. This event will first be a mercy for the Children of Israel, and then it will be a mercy for all of mankind. Through the manifestation of this event, people will attain knowledge of Allah (ma'rifat-e-Ilahi), will worship Him, and will seek His pleasure.

The dialogue between Ruh al-Amin and the Virgin Maryam ends here. What happened after this exchange is not related here. There is an artistic gap in the story at this point, a deliberate pause in the narrative presentation. However, the angel does say clearly that this child will be born of a virgin, that no one will have touched the virgin, that this child will be a miracle for the people and a mercy from Allah, and that the decree has been settled and it shall be so.

Now another scene of the story comes before us: our chaste virgin is presented in a different, astonishing and distressing state. This scene is even more frightening than the first one.

This is the third shock for this chaste maiden. The context does not mention how the pregnancy came about, how long it lasted, or whether it was an ordinary pregnancy such as women normally experience. It was a breath from Allah, and movement arose within the egg in the womb of the woman. It became a clot of blood, bones formed within it, flesh began to grow over the bones, and the foetus completed the appointed term of pregnancy. It may also be that, since movement was produced in the woman's egg, it began its natural process. It is also possible that in this extraordinary event the egg did not complete its usual course, that all these stages were passed quickly, as a marvel, and that the child in the womb completed the stages of development rapidly. The verse contains nothing that tells us which of these two methods and possibilities took place. Therefore we too do not enter into this discussion, for which we have no authentic (musnad) material for research. What is told and shown to us here is only this: the pregnancy took place, and Maryam (ع) went away from her family to a secluded place. Her situation is more frightening for her than her previous situation. In the first stage she was concerned only with her virginity, upbringing and character; this was only her private problem. It could have remained private, but now this matter is about to come before society. Along with psychological distress, she now also suffers physical pain. The pain of labour brings her to the trunk of a date palm. She is compelled to lean on that tree. Here she is alone and without support. The first childbirth of a virgin also involves greater labour pains. She has no experience, and there is no helper or assistant with her, and suddenly these words come from her mouth.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 23:

"Yalaytanee mittu qabla haadha wa kuntu nasyan mansiyyaa" (19:23): "Would that I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten and utterly erased from memory!" The words in which the Qur'an expresses this matter are such that it is as though we are seeing the features of her face; we can practically feel her inner anguish. The sorrow and grief that she is experiencing is something every person truly feels. In such moments, this wish, that her name and trace be wiped away, is permissible.

Mansiyyan (forgotten): it refers to the cloth that is used for menstrual blood and is then thrown away and forgotten (it is thrown in such a place that no one can even see it).

In this intensity of grief and sorrow, suddenly a great surprise is given.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verses 24–25:

O Allah, what sort of child is this? He has just been born, lying on the ground, and yet he is speaking. Now Maryam received comfort with joy. Now she has become connected to her Lord. "O mother, do not grieve. ﴿Your Lord has placed a stream beneath you﴾ (Surah Maryam 19:24) — the stream of water. Fakhtalafa al-ahzab min baynihim (19:37) — "But the various factions among them differed." Qaysar of Rome, Constantine, convened an assembly of priests in which two thousand one hundred and seventy (2170) priests participated. This assembly was one of his three assemblies. In it there was intense disagreement among them about Hazrat Isa. Every sect presented its position. Some said that he is God who descended to the earth, gave life to whomever He wished, caused death to whomever He wished, and then ascended to the heavens. Some people said that he is the Son of Allah; some said that he is one of the three hypostases (aqanim thalatha): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Some said that he is one of three, meaning that Allah is a god, he is a god, and the mother is also a god. Some said that he is a servant of Allah, His spirit, and His word. Apart from these major views, other sects also put forward many opinions. No belief was agreed upon by more than three hundred and seventeen persons. This number gathered around one opinion. The Caesar of Rome inclined towards it, supported those who held that view, and eliminated the others, especially the people of tawhid, whom he utterly destroyed.

Because the wrong beliefs about Hazrat Isa were determined by the assemblies of religious leaders, the context here warns those who adopted beliefs other than tawhid. They are warned of that day, in which more people will gather than in those assemblies, and they will see how dreadful the end of the disbelievers will be.

Lesson No. 631: At a Glance

At the end of the previous lesson, the reality of the birth of Hazrat Isa (peace be upon him) was explained, and it was shown that those who call him the son of God merely hold to illusions, assumptions and stories. They are steeped in great misguidance, and some misguided People of the Book argue from these tales. After this, a portion of the story of Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is presented here, in which the misguidance and falsehood of polytheistic beliefs are made clear. The Arabs and the polytheists of Makkah attribute themselves to Hazrat Ibrahim. The claim of the polytheists of Makkah was that they are the custodians of the House whose construction was carried out by Hazrat Ibrahim and Ismail (peace be upon them both).

In this part of his story, Hazrat Ibrahim appears as a person of most forbearing disposition, and one who is content with the will of Allah. These features of his personality are also well known from his words and his manner of speech, which the Qur'an has related in Arabic. Moreover, his personality is made clear by his actions and by his conduct in confronting his father's ignorance. But Allah also gave him abundant recompense for this character and these qualities. In place of his polytheist father and polytheist family, Allah gave him righteous offspring, from whom a great ummah came into being. In this ummah great prophets and righteous people arose, but after them there also arose unworthy successors who neglected the prayers, followed their carnal desires, and deviated from the path that their forefather Ibrahim had prescribed for them. They even abandoned the religion of Hazrat Ibrahim, and the polytheists of Makkah were the chiefs of these very people.

Allah called Ibrahim (peace be upon him) a siddiq and a prophet. The word siddiq implies both that he was extremely truthful and that he was one who affirmed the truth very much. Both meanings are fitting for the personality of Hazrat Ibrahim.

He speaks to his father with the utmost courtesy and refinement. He is striving that the guidance Allah has given him may benefit his father too, and that he may teach his father the knowledge Allah has bestowed upon him. He addresses his father with great tenderness. "O my father" (ابا جان) is a very gentle form of address.

﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, and which cannot avail you in the least?﴾ (19:42)

The principle of worship is that a person bows before a power that is higher than the human being: one who has greater knowledge and greater strength, and who raises a person above the station of humanity to an even loftier rank. How can a human being worship and serve things that are lower than him? Lesson No. 731: At a Glance

In this surah the story of Prophet Zakariyya (ﷺ) has passed, and the matter of the birth of Prophet Yahya (ﷺ) has also passed. The story of Maryam (ﷺ) and the event of the birth of Prophet Isa (ﷺ) have also passed. The story of Prophet Ibrahim (ﷺ) and his leaving his father and people, and the mention of the people of guidance and the people of misguidance who came after these noble figures, have also passed. After all these narratives, the mention came that the Lord of this universe is One, without partner, and that He alone is deserving of worship. All these stories only manifest this truth: that Allah alone is worthy of worship and servitude.

After this theme, the whole of this lesson now concerns the creed of Tawhid (Oneness of God) and the creed of Ba'th ba'd al-Mawt (resurrection after death). These beliefs are presented in the form of scenes of the Day of Judgment, and these scenes are full of impressions and the bustle of life. Then the whole universe also takes part in these scenes as an audience. All human beings and the whole earth, all human beings and all jinn, both believers and disbelievers, are the characters on the stage in these scenes.

Then these scenes are connected with this world and also move on toward the Day of Resurrection. It appears as though the scenes of both this world and the Hereafter are being shown on one and the same stage. The beginning is from this world, and the ending is shown in the Hereafter in an extremely impactful manner. Between this world and the Hereafter there remains a distance of only a few verses and a few words, through which there arises in the mind of a human being the feeling that this world and that realm are two parts of one stage and one scene.

First, the human being comes onto the stage and states his position regarding resurrection after death. He says a thing that many people have repeated down to today. In different eras, people have said this very thing. It is thus a universal human doubt, and this question has troubled all nations and all races.

﴿And man says: "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ (19:66) "Man says: Is it truly so that when I die, I will be brought out alive again?" This question has arisen in the human heart solely because of his heedlessness. He has not reflected that he exists, and that he was created from nothing; so how could he be doubtful? Where was he, and how was he? Certainly he was not, and then he came into being. If man reflected even a little, he would understand that re-creation is far easier than the first creation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 67:

أَوَلَا يَذْكُرُ الْإِنسَانُ أَنَّا خَلَقْنَاهُ مِن قَبْلُ وَلَمْ يَكُ شَيْئًا ﴿67﴾

"Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?"

Further on, in a tone of warning, the Qur'an addresses this denial and this forced denial. Allah swears by His own Being, and an oath by the Being of Allah is an oath that these people, and all people, will certainly be raised. They will be brought forth and gathered on the Day of Assembly, and this is a decided and settled matter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 68:

"By your Lord, We shall surely gather them, and the devils as well" (91:86). "And they will not be alone. Along with them We shall gather the devils too, because these and the devils are of one kind. It is the devils who instil such doubts into their hearts. The followers are these people, and the devils are their leaders. Between them there is the relationship of follower and followed."

Now, in the next stage, all of them are advancing on their knees. This is a physical picture of their extremely wretched condition.

They are in a state of intense shame and humiliation.

"Then We shall surely bring them around Hell, kneeling" (19:68). "This is a vivid scene: countless people are being assembled, and they are being brought toward Hell in a humiliating manner, on their knees. They look at it helplessly and feel the lashing of its flames. At every moment they are in fear that they will be seized now and thrown into it. In their distress and anguish they move on their knees, and then they are cast down on their faces."

For the tyrants and oppressors of the world, this is an extremely humiliating scene. In this scene, from the ranks of the deniers, those who were more rebellious than the others are being separated out. They are being dragged out from the ranks one by one.

Then We will surely drag out from every group those among them who were most defiant against the Most Merciful. (Qur'an 19:69)

The verse uses an emphatic form with doubled letters, so that the harshness of the word, its intensity, and its emphatic meaning make the act of separating them out even more terrifying. After this comes the casting of them into Hell; the imagination gives practical shape to all these movements.

Allah knows well which of them deserves to be burned in Hell. Therefore, from this vast and countless flood of humanity, He will single them out and bring them forth.

Then We know best who is most deserving of being burned in it. (91:07)

﴿Then We know best who among them is most deserving of being thrown into the Fire.﴾ Allah will bring them out, and they will be the vanguard of those who are cast into Hell. The believers will be watching this scene.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 19, verse 71:

And there is none of you but will pass over it (Hell). This is a decreed matter which your Lord has determined and must fulfil. ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it; that is an absolute decree from your Lord﴾ (19:71). All people will be brought near to Hell, and when they see it, its flames will rise high, will be in turmoil, and will be bursting forth. They will see the disobedient servants being singled out from among the people and being thrown into it.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 19, verse 72:

ثم ننجی الذین اتقوا (91 : 27) ” پھر ہم ان لوگوں کو بچا لیں گے جو دنیا میں متقی تھے “۔ یہ دوزخ ان سے دور ہوجائے گی اور وہ اس میں ڈالے جانے سے بچا لئے جائیں گے اور

ونذر الظلمین فیھا جثیا (91 : 27) ” اور ظالموں کو اس میں گہرا ہوا چھوڑ دیں گے “۔

Then We shall save those who were mindful of God [in the world]. ﴿Then We shall save those who were God-fearing﴾ — [the Hell] will move away from them, and they will be saved from being cast into it, and

﴿And We shall leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling﴾ — "and We shall leave the wrongdoers in it, humbled to their knees."

Now the discourse turns away from that frightening scene, in which the disobedient are being driven along on their knees in utter humiliation, where the God-fearing are delivered and the wrongdoers are left fallen face-down in Hell. Suddenly we are back in the world, where the disbelievers display their own greatness in the face of the believers. They taunt them over their wretched condition. They take pride in their wealth, their outward splendour and their worldly values, although these are things of the perishable abode, values that come to an end.

Great assemblies, gatherings of pleasure and revelry, and the values on which the elites and the affluent of the age act in moral corruption. Set against these are the apparently lower-ranked societies and the gatherings of the poor and destitute, in which there is seldom any equipment other than faith. Moreover, there is little adornment and splendour among them: there are no costly clothes and no costly dwellings. In this world people compete with one another in these very things, and class distinctions are established on their basis.

In this arena of competition and display, at the stall of the first class there are great worldly goods, wealth and beauty, power and status, great allowances, large incomes, and delicious food and drink. At the stall of the second class there is humility and modesty. The equipment that is precious in the eyes of the great is worthless in their sight, and rank and position are worth no more than a straw to them. This second stall does not call people to pleasure and revelry, nor to allowances, nor to influence with the rulers, nor to authority or pride. It calls only to a precious ideological treasure. On this stall there is no costly worldly wealth or property, and no adornment or embellishment. Yet there is the proclaimer of raising the word of Allah on high. This second side calls only to the exaltation of the word of truth. Not only are the worldly things mentioned here absent, but there are hardship, struggle and sacrifices. The reward for all these hardships is not given in this world. Here they will receive only nearness to Allah; as for reward and recompense, that lies in the Hereafter.

These Quraysh, to whom the signs of Allah were being recited in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), used to say, seeing the believing poor:

﴿أَيُّ الْفَرِيقَيْنِ خَيْرٌ مَّقَامًا وَأَحْسَنُ نَدِيًّا﴾ (91 : 37) "Tell us, of the two groups, which is better in station and finer in assembly?" They meant: are the great ones who do not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) better, or are the poor who gather around him better? Whose circumstances are better in worldly terms, and whose society is more splendid? On one side are Nadr ibn al-Harith, Amr ibn Hisham, Walid ibn al-Mughira and their brothers and the other chiefs; on the other side are Bilal, Ammar, Khabbab and their other brothers, who do not have a single cowrie. If the things to which Muhammad (ﷺ) calls were good, then his companions would not be these people, who have no worth or standing in the society of Quraysh. These people all gather together at the house of a wretched Khabbab, who is poor and unemployed. And the opponents of Muhammad (ﷺ) sit in great and splendid assemblies, and they hold high rank in society.

This is the logic and the thinking of the worshippers of the world. In every time and every place, the mode of thought of the worldly and the short-sighted is exactly this. The very wisdom of Allah requires that the Islamic call and those who carry it be free of worldly adornment. Artificial display and colouring must not conceal their true reality. There must be no artifice in anything of theirs. Whoever accepts the leadership of this call should accept it purely for the sake of Allah, and should accept this call. In it there should be no role for the world and the worshippers of the world. There should be no display or greed in it, so that those who seek worldly benefits and worldly gain do not come to it, and so that those who seek worldly adornment, splendour and wealth stay far away.

To startle these self-deceived misguided ones and disbelievers, with their logic and their display of pomp and adornment, and to turn this way of thinking, a sudden jolt is given to their conscience and they are directed to the history of humanity: many peoples in the history of mankind held a similarly apparently splendid position of honour, were intoxicated with the wealth and blessings of the world, yet just look, what was their end?

Here is what happened: their splendour and display did them no good. Their adornments did not save them from the punishment of God. When destruction came upon them, all those outward displays vanished.

Remember, man forgets very quickly. If he had recalled even a little of the lessons of history and reflected even a little, he would never have taken pride in these outward displays. Yet in human history, the nations that were destroyed, their destructions and ruins contain a great store of lessons. Human history seizes man by the hem of his garment and draws him towards itself, saying: look, fear the punishment of God, be wary of the grip of Allah. But man, with his head bowed, continues to walk on his wrong path. He does not look back, so that he may avoid stumbling as he moves forward. Yet those nations of the past who stumbled were more powerful than these, richer than these, and more numerous in population.

But after this fleeting glance, the Qur'an commands the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to tell these people that this intuitive indication is not sufficient for them. Say to them, in a challenging manner: very well, whoever is in error and on a false path, let Allah extend him further in error, until he reaches the end that is the natural outcome of those who go astray, whether in this world or in the Hereafter.

The people think they are on a more correct path than the believers, merely because they are wealthy and have pomp and show. Very well, let their wealth and status be increased further. And O Muhammad (ﷺ), pray against them that they go further and further astray in deviation. May Allah lengthen their rope. He increases those who are guided in guidance, so that these people reach their end, and their end can only be that they are punished at the hands of the Muslims in this world, or that they are punished in the Hereafter. Then they will know the true state of affairs: whose position and rank is good, and who is weak, feeble and helpless. At that time the Muslims will be very happy and will attain honour.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 76:

"And the lasting good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for final outcome" (19:76). They are better than all those things in which the people of the world take pride and are led astray.

Now observe another example of the boasting and vainglory of the disbelievers, another of their statements at which one is astonished and which is strongly rebuked.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 77:

In the occasion of revelation (shan-i nuzul) of this verse, there is a narration from Hadrat Khabbab ibn al-Arat, which says: "I was a blacksmith. Al-As ibn Wa'il owed me a debt. I came to him and demanded my debt. He said: 'By God, I will certainly not give you your debt until you disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ).' I said: 'By God, that will never happen. I cannot deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), even if you die and are resurrected.' He said: 'Very well, when I die and am resurrected, I will have much wealth and children there. Come to me then, and I will give you your debt.' Then Allah revealed this verse."

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieves in Our verses and says, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ (19:77)

The statement of Al-As ibn Wa'il is a prime example of the mockery that the disbelievers of Quraysh directed at the doctrine of resurrection after death. The Qur'an, with astonishment, comments on and takes account of the thinking of such people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 78:

Has he come to know the unseen ("ataala'a al-ghayb") – "Has he come to know the unseen?" That is, does he already know in advance what will happen there?

Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful ("am ittakhadha ... 'ahdan") – "Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" – and he is certain that Allah is bound by His covenant. After this it is said:

"Kalla" – "Certainly not!" Kalla is a word of negation and rebuke. He has neither knowledge of the unseen, nor has he taken any promise from Allah; rather, he has become fixed upon disbelief and is merely mocking. In such places, the fitting response for such disbelievers is that they be given a warning couched in threat.

Kalla, sa-naktubu ma yaqulu... (Qur'an 19:79): "No! We shall record what he says, and We shall extend for him the punishment, lengthening it further." That is, We will record what he says, so that, as is the usual practice, a record is prepared for the Day of Reckoning, so that nothing is forgotten and nothing is left in confusion. This is a most excellent portrayal of threat and warning. Yet confusion (mughalata) could never arise there. The knowledge of Allah does not leave behind the minor nor the major. That is, We will keep lengthening and extending His punishment; there will be no decrease in it and no interruption. Observe further fear and vivid depiction in the manner of the following.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 19, verse 80:

﴿And We shall inherit from him what he speaks of﴾ (19:80): "The wealth and retinue he boasts of will all remain with Us." What he leaves behind in wealth and children, We shall take in the same way that an heir takes possession of what he inherits.

﴿And he will come to Us alone﴾ (19:80): "He will appear before Us alone." He will have no wealth, no children, no helper, and no proof or authority. He will stand before Us alone, weak and helpless. Have you seen the one who denies Our verses and mocks the Day on which he will come empty-handed? In this world, all that he owned will slip out of his hands. This person is the epitome of disbelief and the example of the disbelievers, of denial, of obstinacy, and of misguidance. Now it is explained what the signs of disbelief and polytheism are.

The people who deny the signs of Allah take others besides Allah as gods, seeking through them honour for themselves and seeking from them might and help. Some of them worship the angels, and some worship the jinn and seek help from them. But it can never be so; soon they will deny all their worship, servitude and invocation of these deities, will abhor their actions, and will openly disown them before Allah.

﴿And they will become opponents to them﴾ (91:28). That is, they will disown them and testify against them. The devils who incite them to this deed are ones We have set upon them. Allah has permitted them to lead these people astray, and they have been authorised to do so since the time Iblis asked Allah for respite, saying, "Grant me respite."

﴿And they will become opponents to them﴾ (91:28). That is, they will disown them and testify against them. The devils who incite them to this deed are ones We have set upon them. Allah has permitted them to lead these people astray, and they have been authorised to do so since the time Iblis asked Allah for respite, saying, "Grant me respite."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 84:

﴿So do not be hasty against them.﴾ (91:48) Do not be hasty in seeking the descent of the punishment upon them. Do not let your heart be constricted or worried. These people have been granted only a little respite. Their deeds are being counted, and their account is being kept. The manner of expression indicates that their deeds are being recorded with the utmost precision.

﴿We are only counting out their days for them.﴾ (91:48) What a terrifying warning this is! That person is ruined whose sins and whose deeds, and whose every breath, Allah Himself is keeping account of, and whose account is being recorded with extreme precision, so that he may be seized with severity. The one who feels that during his life on this earth his Creator is watching over his deeds and that his mistakes are being noted, is frightened. He lives in constant fear and in constant apprehension that perhaps at some moment some mistake may be committed by him and not be noted. But the one whose mistakes Allah Himself is noting... One of the scenes of the Day of Resurrection shows the outcome of this counting and reckoning. The condition of the people of faith is that they come to the court of Allah in the form of honoured delegations, with great dignity and respect.

﴿On the Day when We shall gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ (91 : 58) "That is a day that is coming, when We shall present the righteous before the Most Merciful like honoured guests," and We shall drive the guilty toward Hell.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 19, verse 86:

"And We shall drive the criminals to Hell like thirsty cattle." (19:86)

On that Day no one will have the power of intercession, except the one who has taken a promise from the Most Merciful (ʿahd al-Raḥmān). Actually, the translation as given in the source reads: "On that day no one will have any intercession, except for him who did a good deed. That good deed will be his intercessor, and Allah will fulfill His promise. Allah has promised that whoever believes and does righteous deeds, He will give him his full reward, and Allah does not break His promise."

Once again the discourse turns to the false beliefs of the polytheists. Some of the polytheists of Arabia used to say that the angels are the daughters of Allah. A polytheistic section of the Jews used to call ʿUzayr the son of Allah, and the polytheists among the Christians used to say that the Messiah is the son of Allah. Because of these polytheistic statements, the whole universe trembles. The nature of the universe denies them, and the conscience of man recoils from them.

The atmosphere in this scene is one of wrath, jealousy and reaction. The resonance and thunder of the words, and the blows of the phrases and sentences, make this atmosphere even more intense. There is an agitation in the very conscience of the universe. The whole soul of creation is shaken within all its forces that hate such things. Because of such a severe affront to the majesty of the Divine Being, there is intense outrage among all the creative forces. When a person's own self or a beloved person is insulted and their honour is in danger, all their limbs react at once. In the same way, this entire universe is in extreme reaction in this scene, because the honour of its Lord is being insulted.

In reaction to this word of disbelief and this insult to the majesty of God, the whole universe, the earth, the heavens, the trees and the mountains, all are in reaction. And the words the Qur'an has chosen to express this are themselves earth-shaking. Just consider that the moment this word of disbelief is uttered, ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾ (19:88), "They say that the Most Merciful has begotten a son."

Note: The Arabic quotation in the passage is cited as "وکلھم اتیہ یوم القیمۃ فردا (91 : 59)", which is the verse 19:95 (the reference in the source contains a numbering error, given as 91:59).

Every individual is within Allah's sight. Then all of them will come before Allah individually. There will be no group, and no companion or helper. There, the spirit of collectivity and the consciousness of collectivity will be removed from them. Every person will stand before Allah alone, solitary and singular.

In this loneliness, solitude, terror and fear, suddenly a group of the People of Faith appears. They are fresh with Allah's mercy and under the shade of His embrace, extremely happy and joyful, immersed in the affections of the All-Merciful (al-Rahman).

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation) on surah 19, verse 96:

Here, gifts of love perfume the atmosphere. The spirit of Allah's good pleasure permeates within human souls. In the higher realm this spirit holds sway. Then this spirit descends to the earth and spreads among the people. It envelops the entire atmosphere, the whole society, and the whole earth.

It is narrated from Hazrat Abu Hurairah (RA): The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When Allah loves a servant, He calls Jibra'il (AS) and says: "Jibra'il, I love so-and-so, so you too love him." He said: then Jibra'il loves him. Then a herald proclaims among the inhabitants of the heavens: "Listen, Allah loves so-and-so, so you too love him," and the inhabitants of the heavens love him. After this, acceptance is granted to that person on earth. And when Allah hates a servant, He calls Jibra'il and says: "I hate so-and-so, so you too hate him," and Jibra'il hates him. Then a proclamation is made among the inhabitants of the heavens: "Allah hates so-and-so, so you too be hostile to him," and all the inhabitants of the heavens become hostile to him. After this, hatred for him is placed in the whole earth.

After this it is said: This Qur'an is glad tidings for the believers who are pious, and a warning for the deniers and the disputatious. This glad tidings and warning is among the primary purposes of the Holy Qur'an. Allah revealed the Qur'an in Arabic to present it before the Arabs, so that they would recite it, and the Messenger would recite it to them and warn them.

This surah ends on a scene which, on seeing it, makes every person pause for a long time in reflection, and a lasting impression remains within human consciousness and feeling, and a tremor is produced. A person is left thinking and reflects for a long while.

This is a sudden, harsh blow. After it comes a dreadful silence and stillness, as though we stand in a valley of destruction and are looking at each of the valleys that have been laid waste and ruined over the centuries one by one. A long series of destructions is before our eyes. Our thoughts travel along with the lives, the progress and the varied activities of those peoples. Great cities appear, with their populations, and then the movement of life and its bustle can be seen. Then, when Allah's destruction comes upon those settlements, an owl is seen calling there. Life suddenly falls silent, and death alone is visible everywhere. Everywhere there are human corpses, bones, and then black dust. There is no life, no feeling, no movement, no sound.

﴿Do you perceive any one of them, or hear from them even a whisper?﴾ (19:98) Is there any trace or sign? Look carefully at those civilizations. Try to listen closely: this frightening silence, this dreadful stillness. Look here: is there anyone other than Allah, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-Hayy al-Qayyum), the Dominant and the Irresistible (al-Qahhar al-Jabbar)?
